reconcile.connective: Commentators read Isaiah's 'filthy rags' as the fallen self's own righteousness apart from grace, not the Spirit-wrought goodness Luke ascribes to Joseph.

discrepancy.connective: The objection is pressed by Steve Wells in the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, who sets Isaiah's blanket verdict against Luke's flat 'good man' label as flatly incompatible claims.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Is anyone good?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: righteousness--plural, "uncleanness" extended to every particular act of theirs, even to their prayers and praises. True of the best doings of the unregenerate (Phi 3:6-8; Tit 1:15; Heb 11:6).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Restricts the 'filthy rags' verdict to 'the best doings of the unregenerate,' i.e. not a claim about literally every human being — reconciles directly with Luke calling Joseph 'good.'

excerpts.excerpt_text: …not of the righteousness of Christ, which was made hers by imputation; for this is not rags, but a robe, the best robe, and wedding garment … and is opposed to their own righteousness; which is what is intended here, even the best of it …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Distinguishes 'their own righteousness' (filthy rags) from 'the righteousness of Christ...made hers by imputation' (a pure robe) — the imputation move that lets Scripture call a believer 'good' while Isaiah calls unaided human righteousness filthy rags.

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871), on Isaiah 64:6
pd_work.author: Robert Jamieson, A. R. Fausset & David Brown
pd_work.note: JFB treats this exact verse, reading 'filthy rags' as true of 'the best doings of the unregenerate' rather than a categorical verdict on every human being — the harmonizing move this row relies on. (Checked: John Haley's Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible, 1874, does not treat Isaiah 64:6 or this pairing — no 'filthy rags,' 'Joseph of Arimathea,' or '64:6' match in the full text.)
